title: Training Data
blurb: Splits, labelling, leakage, imbalance and augmentation.
source: AWS Certified AI Practitioner (AIF-C01) exam guide · Domain 1
hint: The important distinction is the data's role, format, or fitness for the real population; those details determine what can be learned and whether evaluation is trustworthy.

items.label: Examples that reflect the people, conditions, and cases the model will encounter in use.
items.why: Examples that reflect the people, conditions, and cases the model will encounter in use.

items.label: Information unavailable at prediction time accidentally enters training and inflates measured performance.
items.why: Information unavailable at prediction time accidentally enters training and inflates measured performance.
items.citation: scikit-learn docs · Common pitfalls: data leakage

items.label: One target class appears much more often than another, making accuracy potentially misleading.
items.why: One target class appears much more often than another, making accuracy potentially misleading.
items.citation: AIF-C01 exam guide · Task 4.1 (responsible AI: balanced datasets)

items.label: Attaching ground-truth tags to raw examples so a supervised model has answers to learn from.
items.why: Label quality caps model quality: noisy or inconsistent tags teach the model the wrong mapping no matter how much data there is.
items.citation: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth docs · Data labeling

items.label: The verified correct answer that a model's prediction is compared against during training and evaluation.
items.why: Without a trusted reference answer, neither training loss nor evaluation metrics mean anything — both are measured against it.
items.citation: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth docs · Data labeling

items.label: Creating extra training examples by transforming existing ones, such as flipping images or paraphrasing text.
items.why: It stretches a small dataset and teaches invariance to harmless variation, reducing overfitting without collecting new data.
items.citation: AWS docs · What is data augmentation?

items.label: Artificially generated examples used when real data is scarce, sensitive, or missing rare cases.
items.why: It fills gaps real collection cannot — rare events, privacy-restricted records — but inherits the assumptions of its generator.
items.citation: AWS docs · What is synthetic data?

items.label: Rebalancing a skewed dataset by duplicating or generating additional minority-class examples.
items.why: It gives the rare class enough weight to be learned, at the risk of overfitting to repeated or synthetic minority examples.
items.citation: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler docs · Balance data

items.label: Rebalancing a skewed dataset by discarding some majority-class examples.
items.why: It equalises class influence cheaply, but throws away real signal from the majority class in the process.
items.citation: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler docs · Balance data

items.label: An individual measurable input attribute, such as age, pixel value, or transaction amount, that the model learns from.
items.why: Models only see the features they are given; what is included, and how it is encoded, bounds what can be learned.
items.citation: AIF-C01 exam guide · Task 1.3 (ML development lifecycle: feature engineering)

items.label: Transforming raw inputs into more informative attributes, such as ratios, buckets, or encodings, before training.
items.why: Good derived features let simpler models capture the pattern; poor ones force complex models to rediscover it from noise.
items.citation: AIF-C01 exam guide · Task 1.3 (ML development lifecycle: feature engineering)

items.label: Rotating which slice of data is held out so every example is used for both training and evaluation.
items.why: Averaging over several held-out folds gives a steadier estimate of generalisation than a single split, especially on small datasets.
items.citation: scikit-learn docs · Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance

items.label: Checks on completeness, accuracy, consistency, and freshness applied before data is used to train.
items.why: Defects flow downstream: a model trained on incomplete or inconsistent records encodes those defects as behaviour.
items.citation: AWS Glue Data Quality docs

items.label: Systematic skew introduced when the collection method favours some people or cases over others.
items.why: A model can only be fair to cases it has seen; skewed collection produces skewed predictions however good the algorithm.
items.citation: AIF-C01 exam guide · Task 4.1 (responsible AI: bias and fairness in datasets)

items.label: An extreme or anomalous example that sits far outside the pattern of the rest of the data.
items.why: A handful of extreme points can drag parameters and scaling; deciding whether they are errors or real cases changes the model.
items.citation: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler docs · Handle outliers

items.label: An ordering-aware split where the model trains on earlier periods and is evaluated on later ones.
items.why: Shuffling time series lets the model peek at the future, inflating scores; honest evaluation must respect arrival order.
items.citation: scikit-learn docs · TimeSeriesSplit (time-ordered cross-validation)

items.label: A split that keeps each subset's class proportions the same as the full dataset's.
items.why: Random splits of imbalanced data can starve a fold of the rare class entirely; stratifying keeps every evaluation representative.
items.citation: scikit-learn docs · Stratified sampling in model selection
